segments.narration: Escaped bats burned down an American army airfield in 1943. The bats were armed, and that part was the Army's own idea.
A Pennsylvania dentist had written to the White House a month after Pearl Harbor, proposing bats as incendiary carriers. The plan was approved.
Each casing held 1,040 Mexican free-tailed bats in twenty-six stacked trays, every bat carrying a tiny timed napalm charge. Who signs off on this?
The fire happened during a test at Carlsbad. Observers still called the weapon effective, so the Navy took it over as Project X-Ray.
Two million dollars in, Admiral Ernest King killed it: bat bombs would not be combat-ready before mid-1945. The atomic bomb got there first.

verdicts.claim: On 15 May 1943 armed bats were accidentally released at the Carlsbad Army Airfield Auxiliary Air Base in New Mexico and set fire to the test range.
verdicts.note: 100% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Dental surgeon Lytle S. Adams of Irwin, Pennsylvania proposed the bat bomb in a letter to the White House in January 1942, about a month after Pearl Harbor.
verdicts.note: 94% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The carrier was a sheet-metal tube about 1.5 m long holding 26 trays with 1,040 Mexican free-tailed bats, each fitted with a small timed napalm incendiary developed by Louis Fieser.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: a sheet-metal tube about 1.5 m long with 26 circular trays holding 1,040 bats in total, Mexican free-tailed bats, each carrying a small timed incendiary; Louis Fieser's napalm replaced the original white phosphorus.

verdicts.claim: A National Defense Research Committee observer concluded that 'X-Ray is an effective weapon', and the programme was taken over by the Navy as Project X-Ray.
verdicts.note: 87% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: About $2 million had been spent when Fleet Admiral Ernest J. King cancelled the programme after learning it would probably not be combat-ready until mid-1945.
verdicts.note: 85% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

candidates.text: Escaped bats burned down an American army airfield in 1943
candidates.why: The outcome is absurd and the cause is missing, so the viewer has to stay for why bats were armed.

candidates.text: A dentist talked the White House into weaponising bats
candidates.why: Leads on the unlikely person behind it rather than on what happened.

candidates.text: Each bomb held a thousand bats wearing tiny incendiaries
candidates.why: Pure device detail; vivid, but it explains itself too early.

choice.reason: It states a result nobody can explain away and keeps the real question - who armed them, and why - open until the end.
